name: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)
summary: Sulfur supplement sold for skin, hair and joints; a few small skin trials, but evidence is weak overall.
lead: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM, dimethyl sulfone) is a small organic sulfur compound, (CH3)2SO2, that occurs naturally in trace amounts in some plants, foods and human blood. It is sold as a dietary supplement for joint comfort, skin, hair and nails, and it appears in topical products.
claims: MSM can lighten eye colour at high intake
MSM improves hair texture and strength
MSM relieves joint pain and helps maintain height through the day

name: Hydroxycitric acid (HCA)
summary: Garcinia-derived acid sold as a fat blocker; trials show at most a small short-term weight difference.
lead: Hydroxycitric acid (HCA) is a derivative of citric acid found in the fruit rinds of tropical plants, most notably Garcinia cambogia (Malabar tamarind, also called G. gummi-gutta), and in roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa).  The (-)-isomer found in Garcinia is a competitive inhibitor of ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, which is the basis for its marketing as a fat-loss supplement.

name: Hydroxycut
summary: Mass-market caffeine fat burner with a 2009 FDA warning and recall after liver-injury reports; independent efficacy trials are lacking.
lead: Hydroxycut is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss and fat-burner dietary supplements introduced in 2002 and developed by MuscleTech, a Toronto-area company whose assets were largely sold in 2003-2004 to Iovate Health Sciences, which continues to sell it.  Formulations have changed repeatedly: early versions contained ephedra, later ones included ingredients associated with liver injury, and current products are built around caffeine and plant extracts such as robusta coffee extract.

name: Dexatrim
summary: A long-running diet-pill brand that dropped PPA after stroke concerns and now sells caffeine and green-tea blends with little trial evidence.
lead: Dexatrim is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss products sold as appetite suppressants and energy aids. The line was introduced in the 1970s by Thompson Medical Company and originally relied on phenylpropanolamine (PPA), a sympathomimetic also used in cold remedies . After regulatory action in 2000 PPA was removed, and current capsules are multi-ingredient stimulant blends built around caffeine, green tea extract, ginseng and other botanicals .

name: CortiSlim
summary: A cortisol-themed diet supplement whose advertising drew an FTC false-advertising action and which has no published trials behind it.
lead: CortiSlim is a branded dietary supplement line that was marketed as a "cortisol control" weight-loss formula. It was sold by CortiSlim International and earlier by Window Rock Enterprises, and it combined several herbal blends such as magnolia bark, green tea extract and banana leaf extract .

name: Metabolife
summary: The best-selling ephedra fat burner of its era, ended by cardiovascular safety concerns, litigation, a federal ephedra ban and bankruptcy.
lead: Metabolife was a San Diego company founded in the 1990s by Michael Ellis, best known for Metabolife 356, an ephedra- and caffeine-based weight-loss and energy supplement sold largely through a customer-driven distribution model . At its peak it was the top-selling dietary weight-loss supplement in the United States .

name: Chromium nicotinate
summary: A niacin-bound chromium supplement sold for fat loss and glucose control; trials of chromium forms show no reliable body-composition benefit.
lead: Chromium nicotinate (chromium polynicotinate) is a form of trivalent chromium bound to niacin, sold as a dietary supplement alongside chromium picolinate and chromium chloride. Chromium products have been marketed for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control .

name: Policosanol
summary: A sugarcane-wax alcohol mixture sold for cholesterol, with disputed lipid results and no evidence on body fat or looks.
lead: Policosanol is a mixture of long-chain primary alcohols, chiefly octacosanol, extracted from plant waxes such as sugarcane wax and sold as a cholesterol-lowering dietary supplement . It was first developed commercially in Cuba . It is not an appearance compound; the wiki lists it among fat- and metabolism-related supplements.

name: Red yeast rice
summary: Fermented rice containing natural lovastatin, studied for cholesterol; contents are inconsistent and it has no evidence for looks.
lead: Red yeast rice is rice fermented with the mold Monascus purpureus. It has long been used in Chinese cooking and traditional medicine and is now sold as a supplement for cholesterol . It contains monacolins, including monacolin K, which is chemically identical to the drug lovastatin .

name: Fucoidan
summary: A brown-seaweed sulfated sugar sold as a longevity supplement; lab results are plentiful, human appearance data absent.
lead: Fucoidan is a group of sulfated polysaccharides, built largely from the sugar fucose, found in the cell walls of brown seaweeds and in a few marine invertebrates such as sea cucumbers and sea urchins. Commercial material is usually extracted from species including Fucus vesiculosus, Laminaria japonica (kombu), Undaria pinnatifida (wakame) and Cladosiphon okamuranus. Its structure varies with species, season and extraction method, which makes products hard to compare.

name: Cycloastragenol
summary: A purified astragalus saponin marketed as a telomerase activator; mostly cell and animal data, no appearance trials.
lead: Cycloastragenol is a tetracyclic triterpenoid obtained from the roots of Astragalus species, notably Astragalus membranaceus. It is the aglycone (sugar-free form) of astragaloside IV, a major saponin of the herb used in traditional Chinese medicine. It is marketed as a supplement ingredient on the claim that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes.

name: Astragalus
summary: The root behind huangqi, a classic Chinese tonic herb; promoted for longevity and immunity, with no appearance trials.
lead: Astragalus, in this entry, refers to the root of Astragalus membranaceus (also Astragalus mongholicus or A. propinquus), known in traditional Chinese medicine as huangqi. It is a perennial legume native to temperate Asia, and the root is one of the best-known tonic herbs in Chinese and Mongolian traditional medicine. It is promoted in the longevity-supplement category as an immune and anti-ageing tonic.

name: Gynostemma pentaphyllum (jiaogulan)
summary: A sweet adaptogen tea vine with ginseng-like saponins; lab-rich, human data thin, no appearance trials.
lead: Gynostemma pentaphyllum, called jiaogulan or "five-leaf ginseng", is a climbing vine in the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) native to South and East Asia and New Guinea. It is usually drunk as a sweet herbal tea and also sold as extracts and supplements, and is grouped with adaptogen herbs in the longevity category.

name: Schisandra chinensis
summary: The five-flavour berry of Chinese and Russian tonic tradition; liver and antioxidant lab data, nothing on looks.
lead: Schisandra chinensis, the Chinese magnolia vine or five-flavour berry (wuweizi in Chinese, omija in Korean), is a deciduous woody vine native to forests of northern China, the Russian Far East, Korea and Japan. Its red berries are used in traditional medicine and in a Korean cordial drink, and the extract is sold as an adaptogen in the longevity-supplement category.

name: Rhodiola rosea
summary: The Arctic adaptogen root sold for stress and fatigue; mixed-quality trials and nothing on appearance.
lead: Rhodiola rosea, known as golden root, rose root or Arctic root, is a perennial succulent in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that grows in cold, high-altitude and Arctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America. Its rhizome is used in traditional medicine and sold as an adaptogen: a supplement promoted for stress, fatigue and stamina.
claims: Rhodiola may affect estrogen and testosterone
Anything that boosts productivity abruptly is best avoided, like energy drinks

name: Eleutherococcus (Siberian ginseng)
summary: A thorny Asian shrub root sold as a stress-and-fatigue adaptogen; human evidence is thin and nothing ties it to appearance directly.
lead: Eleutherococcus senticosus, commonly called Siberian ginseng or eleuthero, is a thorny deciduous shrub of the family Araliaceae native to eastern Asia, including China, Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East. Despite the common name it is not a true ginseng: it belongs to a different genus from Panax species such as Asian and American ginseng.
claims: Eleuthero is an adaptogen that raises resistance to stress and fatigue
Siberian ginseng is equivalent to true ginseng
Adaptogens improve skin or looks by lowering stress

name: Rhaponticum carthamoides (maral root)
summary: A Siberian herb rich in ecdysteroids that is sold as a muscle and adaptogen supplement; no human trial backs the muscle claims.
lead: Rhaponticum carthamoides (synonym Leuzea carthamoides), known as maral root, is a perennial herb of the daisy family (Asteraceae) that grows wild in southern Siberia, Kazakhstan, the Altai and the western Sayan Mountains at sub-alpine and alpine elevations. Its roots are rich in 20-hydroxyecdysone, an ecdysteroid that acts as a molting hormone in arthropods.
claims: Maral root's ecdysteroids build muscle and aid recovery

name: Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi / Lingzhi)
summary: Traditional East Asian medicinal mushroom sold for immunity and sleep; clinical evidence is poor and nothing addresses appearance.
lead: Ganoderma lucidum, known as reishi in Japan and lingzhi in China, is a bracket fungus used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, in which it was regarded as a mushroom promoting health and longevity. It is taken as tea, extract or capsules and is marketed in wellness and recovery circles as an immune, sleep and stress aid.
claims: Reishi improves immunity and fights disease
Reishi products contain real G. lucidum

name: Royal jelly
summary: Bee-larvae food sold as a skin and wellness supplement; EFSA found no support for human claims and no trial covers appearance.
lead: Royal jelly is a milky secretion produced by the head glands of young worker honey bees (Apis mellifera) and fed to all larvae in their first days and, throughout life, to queen larvae and adult queens. It is harvested commercially and sold as a dietary supplement and a cosmetic ingredient, and is used in apitherapy.

name: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol)
summary: Pine-bark polyphenol antioxidant floated for skin and melasma; Cochrane found insufficient evidence for other uses and no skin trial turned up.
lead: Pycnogenol is the trademarked name of a standardised extract of French maritime pine (Pinus pinaster) bark, composed mainly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins, about 70%). The term was coined in 1979 by chemist Jack Masquelier, who had extracted proanthocyanidins from pine bark.

name: Grape seed extract
summary: A grape-derived procyanidin antioxidant; the appearance case rests on lab data, with no trials on skin or looks.
lead: Grape seed extract (GSE) is a dietary supplement made from the seeds of grapes, mainly Vitis vinifera, which are a by-product of winemaking and grape-juice production. Its polyphenol fraction, typically 5-8% of the seed by weight, consists largely of flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin and their oligomers and polymers, known as procyanidins or oligomeric proanthocyanidin complexes.
claims: Grape seed extract works as an aromatase inhibitor and so can lower estrogen.

name: Genistein
summary: A soy phytoestrogen studied for many conditions; no trials test it for skin or looks.
lead: Genistein is an isoflavone, a type of plant phytoestrogen, found mainly in soybeans and other legumes. It was first isolated from dyer's broom (Genista tinctoria) in 1899 and has the formula C15H10O5.

name: Diosmin
summary: A citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling; interest for face puffiness is untested.
lead: Diosmin is a flavonoid glycoside (diosmetin 7-O-rutinoside) found in citrus fruit and first isolated in 1925; it is made commercially by converting hesperidin from citrus peel.

name: Krill oil
summary: A phospholipid-bound omega-3 supplement that raises blood EPA/DHA; its skin and looks effects are untested.
lead: Krill oil is a supplement extracted from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), a small crustacean. It supplies the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA largely bound to phospholipids, along with the carotenoid astaxanthin.

name: Sodium beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB salts)
summary: Ketone-salt supplements raise blood BHB; fat-loss and looks claims have not been tested.
lead: Sodium beta-hydroxybutyrate is a salt form of beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), the main ketone body the liver makes during fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate diets.  In supplements, BHB is bound to sodium, potassium, magnesium or calcium; most products are racemic, so only about half is the biologically used D form.

name: Ketone monoester (R-1,3-butanediol ester)
summary: The most-studied ketone drink; it lowers appetite hormones in one study, but fat-loss results are unpublished.
lead: The ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate is a drink that raises blood D-beta-hydroxybutyrate quickly. It was developed at the US National Institutes of Health by Richard Veech and Todd King and later sold by companies including KetoneAid, TDeltaS and HVMN, according to Wikipedia.

name: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate
summary: A ketone triglyceride (3GHB) that releases beta-hydroxybutyrate; human work so far is limited to pharmacokinetic studies.
lead: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate (3GHB, also tri-betahydroxybutyrin) is a synthetic triglyceride in which glycerol is fully esterified with beta-hydroxybutyric acid, a ketone body. It has the formula C15H26O9 and is a water-soluble clear oil. It is not itself a ketone.

name: R-1,3-butanediol
summary: A diol the body converts into the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate; human evidence for appearance or fat loss is not established in the sources.
lead: 1,3-Butanediol (C4H10O2) is a diol and secondary alcohol, a bittersweet water-soluble liquid used as a solvent, flavor-additive carrier, and intermediate for resins. The (R) enantiomer has CAS number 6290-03-5. In the exogenous ketone field, R-1,3-butanediol is described as a compound that significantly raises blood ketone levels and is a component of ketone esters developed at the NIH by Richard Veech and Todd King.

name: Alanyl-glutamine
summary: A stable glutamine dipeptide studied mainly in hospital nutrition, with no trials found for physique or appearance goals.
lead: Alanyl-glutamine (L-alanyl-L-glutamine) is a synthetic dipeptide used as a glutamine source in clinical nutrition. A 1989 randomized Lancet study in 12 patients after colorectal cancer surgery gave it in parenteral nutrition and examined muscle glutamine loss and nitrogen balance.

name: Glutamine
summary: The most abundant amino acid in blood, sold as a muscle-recovery supplement; its clinical evidence lies in medicine, not physique.
lead: Glutamine (Gln, Q) is an alpha-amino acid used in protein synthesis and the most abundant free amino acid in human blood. It is classed as non-essential but conditionally essential, because demand can exceed supply during stress such as illness or injury. Roughly 90 percent of it is made in muscle tissue, and the intestines, kidneys, activated immune cells and many cancer cells use it heavily.
